title: Your younger self

segments.voice: Yesterday, family feuds, and Moses praying for the sister who spoke against him. Your line was one step. Did you find the smallest one? Today, someone you've known longer than anyone: the person you used to be. Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

An old notebook turns up in a box during a move. The handwriting is yours, but the person writing isn't quite. There's the plan to marry someone who turned out to be a disaster. There's the cruel joke about a friend. There's the decision that cost a job, or a year, or a relationship. Some people laugh at their old notebooks. Some people close them fast. Earlier this block we talked about forgiving yourself in general. Today is narrower: the younger one, who had less to work with. Two lines from the Bible can be read as speaking to that person.
screen: `AN OLD NOTEBOOK.` → `YOUR HANDWRITING, NOT QUITE YOU.` → `THE YOUNGER ONE.`

segments.voice: First, a stage, not a verdict. Paul, writing to the church at Corinth, says: "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things." Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say the child was wicked. He says the child understood as a child. The younger self had a smaller map, and acted inside it. Second, a prayer about youth. Psalm twenty-five asks: "Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: according to thy mercy remember thou me for thy goodness' sake, O LORD." Look at the two rememberings. Don't remember the sins. Do remember me. The psalmist isn't asking to be excused. He's asking to be seen as more than the worst of his younger days. Third, the trick of hindsight. Looking back, the warning signs are obvious, because now you know how it ended. Your younger self didn't. Blaming them for not knowing the ending is a bit like shouting at a character in a movie you've already seen. Your line today is a plain statement of that fact. Fourth, what the line is not. I didn't know then is not the same as it didn't matter. If someone was hurt, earlier this block gave us amends: make it right where you can. Forgiving your younger self doesn't cancel the repair. It just sets down the blame, so the person you are now has the energy to do the repairing.
screen: `A CHILD UNDERSTANDS AS A CHILD.` · `REMEMBER NOT THE SINS. REMEMBER ME.` · `HINDSIGHT KNOWS THE ENDING.` · `FORGIVEN, AND STILL REPAIRING.` · then, large: `I DIDN'T KNOW THEN.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a younger you, at a particular age, in a particular room. See the clothes, the hair, the phone or the lack of one. Recall one thing that version of you did that still stings. Now, instead of looking at the mistake, look at the person. What did they know? What were they afraid of? Who was teaching them? Let them be young. If it feels right, say your line silently to them, or about them: I didn't know then. If you pray, you can hold that younger self in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Corinth. The church Paul wrote to, saying when he was a child he understood as a child, before he put away childish things. Today's word.
Your line: I didn't know then. When an old memory makes you wince today, try saying it, and then ask what you know now that you can use. Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray the Psalms, including Psalm 25 with its request not to remember the sins of youth; Christians read Paul's line about childish things as part of his chapter on love, 1 Corinthians 13.

myth: Paul calls the child he was wicked
he says he spoke, understood and thought as a child, then put childish things away.

"remember not the sins of my youth… remember thou me."

fork.setup: you're the psalmist, thinking about what you did when you were young. what do you ask for?
options: that it be excused because you were young.
that the sins be forgotten and you be remembered.
that you never be reminded of it again.
fork.reveal: Psalm 25 uses remember twice: remember not the sins, and remember thou me, by mercy.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiving your younger self means saying it didn't matter.
what it means: seeing that they acted on what they knew, and still repairing what you can.
what a scholar hears: Psalm 25:7 uses remember twice, remember not the sins, remember thou me, and asks that the remembering be by mercy.

notes: Trapdoor third floor: in English (KJV) 'remember' appears twice in Psalm 25:7; the Hebrew uses the root zakhar in both places. Confirm before keeping 'one verb'.
Paul's line is about mature love in context (1 Corinthians 13); applying it to forgiving the younger self is a reading, framed as such.
